summary: Collects experience from building ENUM systems, which map telephone numbers to internet identifiers using DNS, and from the ENUM data others have created. It clarifies the ENUM and DDDS specifications and points out pitfalls so later implementers can avoid them.

plainLanguage.summary: ENUM lets you look up a phone number the way you look up a website name. This note is a list of lessons from people who built it, to help newcomers avoid the same mistakes.

questions: how does enum sort naptr records
subtitle: Lessons from real ENUM software and zones, and the pitfalls to avoid when mapping phone numbers through DNS.

tldr.problem: ENUM maps telephone numbers to URIs using DNS NAPTR records, but implementers read the ENUM and DDDS standards differently, so real clients and zones disagree on details like character sets, sort order and non-terminal records.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reports what implementers saw in the field, clarifies the standards text, and gives SHOULD and MUST advice separately for provisioning systems and for ENUM clients.
tldr.outcome: It does not revise the standards. It is Informational input for future revisions of the ENUM and DDDS specifications.

facts.label: Loop detection threshold
facts.value: More than 5 domains in one query

today: RFC 5483 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not define a standard, and it says it is intended as input to future revisions of the ENUM and DDDS documents.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
RFC 5483 captures experience from building systems based on the ENUM protocol and from looking at ENUM data that others created. Its goal is to clarify the ENUM and Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) standards. It does not revise them, but it is meant as technical input to future revisions and as advice on pitfalls.

The DNS is ENUM's database. ENUM stores its DDDS rules in NAPTR (Naming Authority Pointer) resource records. The RFC assumes the reader already knows the core ENUM specification (RFC 3761) and the DDDS specifications, and it says plainly that other implementers may make different choices.
sections.plainLanguage: Many people built phone-number lookup software from the same instruction book, but they understood some pages differently. This note explains where they got confused.

sections.title: Character Sets, Case and Delimiters
sections.content:
NAPTR records may carry Unicode in UTF-8, which trips up software that handles strings one byte at a time. The RFC walks through each NAPTR field and finds that only the Regexp field could realistically hold non-ASCII text. Its advice is that ENUM NAPTRs SHOULD NOT include characters outside the printable US-ASCII range. If an internationalised domain name or IRI is needed, it should be converted with Punycode or the IRI-to-URI mapping.

The case-insensitivity flag i is pointless for ENUM, because the expression only runs over a + followed by digits, so it SHOULD NOT be provisioned. The delimiter in the Regexp field should be !, and a literal ! inside the field MUST be escaped with a backslash. A literal + in the regular expression MUST also be escaped as \+.

Leaving + unescaped makes an invalid expression, yet this is a common mistake. The obsolete RFC 2916 even printed an example with this error.
sections.plainLanguage: Stick to plain keyboard letters and numbers in these records, and put a backslash in front of special symbols so computers do not mistake them for instructions.

sections.title: Sorting and Processing NAPTRs
sections.content:
A client sorts the NAPTRs it gets back, using ORDER as the major sort term and PREFERENCE/PRIORITY as the minor one, lowest first. It then checks each record: the Flags field, the E2U application identifier in Services, and whether the regular expression matches the queried number. Records that fail are discarded and the next one is tried. A client that does not support an Enumservice, such as one that only does SIP, can skip a record offering H323.

In practice many clients use local knowledge, such as a URI that does not resolve or is a premium-rate number, to skip to a record with a worse ORDER. Strictly this is non-compliant, but the RFC calls it almost universal and understandable. So registrants SHOULD NOT rely on clients obeying ORDER alone and should list only contacts they are willing to support.

  • Records with identical ORDER and PRIORITY give indeterminate behaviour and SHOULD NOT be provisioned unless they are truly equal.
  • Provisioning SHOULD use a default ORDER; the RFC recommends 100.
  • A compound NAPTR such as E2U+voice:tel+sms:tel should be processed left to right.
sections.plainLanguage: Records come with a ranking, like a list of phone numbers to try in order. Some programs skip ahead when a number is obviously broken, so do not list anything you would not want called.

sections.title: Non-Terminal NAPTRs
sections.content:
A non-terminal NAPTR has an empty Flags field and points to another domain that holds more NAPTRs, so a query can follow a chain of domains. The RFC argues that this is hard on both sides. Management systems must validate records in domains they may not control, and clients face sequential DNS queries of unpredictable duration plus the risk of loops. Some clients ignore such records, so non-terminal NAPTRs SHOULD NOT be used unless every client in the environment supports them.

Where they are used, the target domain MUST be in the non-empty Replacement field, the Regexp field MUST be empty and ignored by clients, and the Services field SHOULD be empty. ORDER and PRIORITY values apply only within the domain being processed. A client MAY treat a chain of more than 5 domains in one query as a loop, and then SHOULD skip to the next NAPTR in the referring domain without making the query.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a record just says "look over there instead". That can send programs around in circles, so people should only do it if everyone's software knows how to follow the signs.

sections.title: Old Syntax and Collected Advice
sections.content:
The original ENUM specification, RFC 2916, put the protocol sub-field before the E2U tag in the Services field. RFC 3761 reversed it so that E2U comes first, followed by one or more Enumservices separated by +. ENUM clients MUST support the RFC 3761 form and SHOULD also accept the obsolete form, while zones MUST NOT be provisioned with it. IANA should reject any Enumservice registered with the label E2U.

Sections 7 and 8 collect all the advice into two lists, one for provisioning systems and one for clients. Clients MUST be ready, without failing, to meet other delimiters, non-trivial expressions, application identifiers other than E2U, and many back-reference patterns. If one NAPTR is discarded, the whole query SHOULD NOT end; processing continues with the next record.
sections.plainLanguage: An old way of writing the records still exists in the wild. New software should be able to read both, but people should only write the new way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The clarifications are not expected to add security risk beyond the normative ENUM documents. Two points do matter. Following non-terminal NAPTRs can loop, and the limit of 5 domains is a valid defence, though a tight loop between two domains is traversed 5 times before it is detected.

Regular-expression rewriting can also cause buffer overruns when a Repl sub-field repeats back-reference patterns. Provisioning designers SHOULD limit repeated back-references. Client implementers SHOULD avoid fixed character buffers and MUST NOT fail when a buffer is exhausted.
sections.plainLanguage: A tricky record could try to make a program write more than it has room for, or send it around in circles. Programs should count their steps and leave plenty of room.

viz.caption: WRONG AND CORRECT NAPTR FROM THE RFC

data.title: Escaping the plus sign
data.code:
Incorrect:
* IN NAPTR 100 10 "u" "E2U+sip" "!^+4655(.*)$!sip:\\1@example.net!" .

Correct:
* IN NAPTR 100 10 "u"
    "E2U+sip" "!^\\+4655(.*)$!sip:\\1@example.net!" .
